sections.title: Management

pairs.value: Quickly check for IV thrombolysis &/or thrombectomy; se decisions are timecritical & involve neurology/stroke team now
Standard for LVO within 0-6h when imaging/severity fit (commonly NIHSS >6, ASPECTS >6); selected pts can treated out to 24h if perfusion imaging shows salvageable tissue.
If eligible for both within 4.5h, give IV thrombolysis & proceed to thrombectomy; thrombolysis not delay thrombectomy & not be skipped in eligible pts.

Prethrombolysis/thrombectomy: <185/110. First 24h after thrombolysis: <180/105. After thrombolysis: commonly maintain SBP 140-180. After thrombectomy: avoidlow SBP (<120). If no reperfusion thetherapy, avoid routine BP lowering unless >=220/120, then reduce ~15% initially.
Treat fever, maintain euvolemia, correct glucose abnormalities, & avoid hypoxia & ↓ BP
If no thrombolysis, start antiplatelet therapy after hemorrhage is excluded; if thrombolysis is given, avoid antiplatelets/anticoagulants for 24 hours

If noncardioembolic minor stroke (NIHSS <=3) or high risk TIA (ABCD2 >=4) without thrombolysis/thrombectomy, start aspirin + clopidogrel within 24h & continue 21-30 days, then transition to single antiplatelet thetherapy.
STAT Noncon head CT; CTA head/neck with perfusion imaging if considering thrombectomy
POC glucose, CBC, BMP/CMP, PT/INR, aPTT, troponin
ECG telemetry; look for AFib or concurrent ischemia
Swallow screen, lipid panel, A1c, TTE as part of inpt stroke workup

items: Underlying cause: malignancy (primary or metastatic), recent stroke or TBI, hypertensive emergency, hepatic failure, meningitis/abscess, post-neurosurgical
Rate of decline: sudden (hemorrhage, herniation) vs gradual (tumor, hydrocephalus)
Known ICP monitor or EVD already in place?

pairs.value: Temporal lobe pushes uncus over tentorium → CN III compression → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil + down-and-out gaze → contralateral hemiplegia. Classic sign of impending herniation.
Bilateral downward displacement of diencephalon → bilateral small reactive pupils (early) → fixed mid-position pupils → Cheyne-Stokes breathing → decorticate then decerebrate posturing.
Cerebellar tonsils pushed through foramen magnum → direct brainstem compression → sudden apnea, cardiovascular collapse, death. Can be precipitated by LP in setting of elevated ICP.
Cingulate gyrus herniates under falx cerebri → ACA compression → contralateral leg weakness. Often precedes transtentorial herniation.
Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respirations. Late sign of critically elevated ICP with brainstem compression. Treat immediately — do not wait for the full triad.
Blood-brain barrier breakdown: brain tumors (primary or metastatic), brain abscess, meningitis, contusion. Responds to dexamethasone.
Intracellular water accumulation from cellular energy failure: ischemic stroke, hypoxic-ischemic injury, hyponatremia, hepatic encephalopathy. Does NOT respond to steroids.
CSF forced into periventricular white matter from obstructive hydrocephalus. Treat with EVD or shunt.
ICH, subdural hematoma, epidural hematoma, SAH with hydrocephalus — may need urgent surgical evacuation.
Hyponatremia (acute Na <125), hyperammonemia, DKA, rapid glucose correction, dialysis disequilibrium syndrome.
Bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, cerebral abscess, autoimmune encephalitis, PRES.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (Na+, osm, glucose), coags, ABG, ammonia (if hepatic), LFTs
-**Orders:** CT head non-contrast STAT, arterial line, Foley, HOB 30°, neurosurgery consult, ICU admission
Recognize herniation early: unequal pupils, posturing, Cushing's triad, declining GCS, effaced cisterns on CT
Airway: intubate if GCS ≤8 or unable to protect airway; RSI with rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg
Ventilator targets: SpO2 >94%, PaCO2 35-40 mmHg (normocapnia); hyperventilate to PCO2 30-35 mmHg ONLY as a bridge during active herniation (max 30-60 min)
Hemodynamic targets: MAP ≥80, CPP 60-70 mmHg; use norepinephrine if MAP insufficient
Position: HOB 30°, head and neck midline, avoid internal jugular compression (tight cervical collars)
Hyperosmolar therapy — choose one:
- Mannitol 1 g/kg IV bolus (20% solution); repeat q4-6h PRN; STOP if serum osm >320 mOsm/kg
- 23.4% NaCl 30 mL IV bolus via central line (most potent, fastest)
- 3% NaCl 250 mL IV over 20 min (peripheral-safe alternative)
Steroids: dexamethasone 10 mg IV load then 4 mg q6h ONLY for vasogenic edema (tumor, abscess) — NOT for stroke, TBI, or hemorrhage
Normothermia: treat fever aggressively (each 1°C rise ↑ ICP ~5-7%); acetaminophen + cooling blanket
Normoglycemia: glucose 140-180 mg/dL; avoid both hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia
Avoid hypo-osmolar fluids: no free water, D5W, or 0.45% NS — worsen cerebral edema
Seizure prophylaxis: levetiracetam 1000-1500 mg IV for TBI, hemorrhage, abscess; cEEG if unexplained deterioration
EVD: for hydrocephalus or ICP monitoring with CSF drainage — neurosurgery places
Decompressive craniectomy: for malignant MCA infarction (age <60, within 48h) or refractory TBI

pairs.value: Target ICP <20-22 mmHg. Treat if ICP >20-25 mmHg sustained >5 min.
CPP = MAP - ICP. Target CPP 60-70 mmHg. CPP <50 mmHg associated with poor outcomes.
Maintain MAP ≥80 mmHg. Avoid SBP <90 (doubles TBI mortality). Norepinephrine is vasopressor of choice.
Stop mannitol if serum osm >320 mOsm/kg. Check q6h during therapy.
Target Na 145-155 mEq/L for refractory ICP with hypertonic saline. Check Na q4-6h. Max correction rate 10 mEq/L per 24h.
HOB 30° + midline → osmotherapy → brief hyperventilation (PCO2 30-35) → neurosurgery (EVD / OR) → vasopressors for MAP ≥80

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
drugs.contraindications: Serum osm >320, renal failure, hypovolemia
drugs.notes: Repeat q4-6h PRN. Check serum osm q6h. Stop if osm >320. Causes brief transient ICP rise on infusion. Requires Foley.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 23.4%
drugs.dose: 30 mL IV bolus via central line
drugs.contraindications: Na >155 mEq/L
drugs.notes: Most potent osmotherapy for acute herniation. Central line required — causes severe tissue necrosis peripherally. Onset ~5 min.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3%
drugs.dose: 250 mL IV over 20 min; maintenance 0.1-1 mL/kg/hr
drugs.contraindications: Na >155 mEq/L
drugs.notes: Can give peripherally. Target Na 145-155 for refractory ICP. Check Na q4-6h.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.dose: 10 mg IV load, then 4 mg IV q6h
drugs.contraindications: Ischemic stroke, TBI, ICH (no benefit; may worsen outcomes)
drugs.notes: ONLY for vasogenic edema from tumor or abscess. NOT indicated for stroke, TBI, or cytotoxic edema.

drugs.name: Rocuronium
drugs.dose: 1.2 mg/kg IV for RSI; 0.6 mg/kg for standard NMB
drugs.contraindications: Neuromuscular disease (myasthenia gravis — use cautiously), difficult airway without rescue plan
drugs.notes: Preferred NMB for RSI in elevated ICP. Avoid succinylcholine if hyperkalemia risk. Reversal: sugammadex 16 mg/kg.

drugs.name: Levetiracetam
drugs.dose: 1000-1500 mg IV load over 15 min; maintenance 500-1500 mg IV/PO q12h
drugs.contraindications: Renal failure (dose-adjust), hypersensitivity; psychiatric side effects
drugs.notes: Seizure prophylaxis in TBI, hemorrhage, abscess. Renally dosed. Well-tolerated; no significant drug interactions.

drugs.name: Norepinephrine
drugs.contraindications: Hypovolemia (volume-resuscitate first); mesenteric ischemia (relative)
drugs.notes: Vasopressor of choice to maintain MAP ≥80 and CPP ≥60. Titrate to MAP goal, not a fixed dose.

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: A blown fixed dilated pupil = uncal herniation until proven otherwise: treat before CT if clinical picture fits
Cushing's triad is a late sign — act before the full triad appears
Hyperventilation is a bridge only: sustained hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia beyond 30-60 min
Mannitol causes a brief transient ICP rise (~5 min) before effect kicks in — warn the team
Do NOT use dexamethasone for ischemic stroke, TBI, or ICH: increases infection, hyperglycemia, and mortality
Hyponatremia aggravates cerebral edema: check Na q4-6h and correct at max 8-10 mEq/L per 24h to avoid central pontine myelinolysis
LP is CONTRAINDICATED in suspected transtentorial herniation or markedly elevated ICP: may precipitate tonsillar herniation
Fever is catastrophic in elevated ICP: treat aggressively with acetaminophen + cooling blanket

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (glucose, Na+, Ca2+), CBC, AED levels (if on AEDs), toxicology screen, ABG/VBG (if prolonged)
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, EEG (if altered after seizure stops), CT head (if new-onset or focal), telemetry, neurology consult
If safe, video event for neuro review
**Lorazepam 4 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg) q5 min x2-3**
No IV > midazolam IM/IN/buccal or diazepam PR
0-5 min: ABCs, IV, POC glucose, O2, thiamine if at risk
RSI if needed; ketamine or propofol reasonable
Still seizing after 5-10 min > repeat benzo
10-40 min > levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate, or lacosamide
Refractory SE > intubate, ICU, EEG, anesthetic infusion
Superrefractory SE > neurocritical care; autoimmune / rescue options
Correct cause: glucose, Na, Ca, infection, withdrawal, toxin, structural lesion
After control > telemetry, pulse ox, neuro checks; EEG / MRI / LP as needed
**Stat:** POC glucose, IV access, iStat/VBG, BMP, Mg, Phos, CBC
**Routine:** LFTs, CK, lactate, INR, UA, ECG, telemetry
**Helpful adjuncts:** Early lactate supports recent generalized tonicclonic seizure; prolactin occasionally helpful
**Consider:** CXR, betahCG, tox studies, AED levels, CT head, MRI brain, urgent EEG
**Image now if firsttime / high risk:** First seizure + persistent AMS, focal deficit, trauma, anticoagulation, immunocompromise, malignancy, fever, severe HA, bleed / mass / stroke concern
**If febrile / immunocompromised / unclear cause:** LP, blood cultures, empiric CNS infection coverage
**If PNES likely:** Exclude mimics; once stable, avoid repeated anticonvulsants or invasive escalation for atypical persistent events

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Classic triad: mental status changes + neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor) + autonomic instability within 24h of starting or increasing a serotonergic agent — clonus is the hallmark finding
Clonus: spontaneous, inducible (ankle), or ocular (hallmark finding)
Hyperreflexia: esp lower extremities
Tremor, myoclonus, agitation
Diaphoresis, mydriasis (dilated pupils), flushing
Hypertonia/rigidity (more prominent in lower extremities)
Temp >38°C, tachycardia, HTN, tachypnea

pairs.value: Leadpipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, slow onset (days–weeks), dopamine blocker exposure. CKmuch higher.
Volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine exposure. OR/PACU setting. Hypercarbia is earliest sign.
Dry skin (no diaphoresis), urinary retention, absent bowel sounds. SS has diaphoresis & hyperactive bowels
Cocaine, amphetamines. Similar autonomic findings but no clonus or hyperreflexia
Fever, AMS, nuchal rigidity. LP required to differentiate.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP, CBC, CK (rhabdomyolysis), LFTs, coags (DIC if severe), ABG/VBG (if respiratory compromise)
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, telemetry, stop all serotonergic agents, toxicology consult
Agitation & tremors: **lorazepam 2 mg IV** (benzos are first line)
!!Severe sx!!: **cyproheptadine 12 mg PO/NG load**: 4 mg PO q2h until improvement (max 32 mg/day)
Cooling blanket/Ice for hyperthermia !!avoid acetamenaphen!! (not effective in drug induced hyperthermia)

**Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria**: serotonergic agent + any one of following: spontaneous clonus; inducible clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; ocular clonus + agitation or diaphoresis; tremor + hyperreflexia; or hypertonia + temperature >38°C + ocular or inducible clonus
**Immediate**: Stop all serotonergic agents. Most cases improve within 24h after stopping drug, though long 1/2 life meds may last longer.
**Mild** (tremor, hyperreflexia): Supportive care, remove precipitating drugs, & use benzodiazepines for agitation/tremor.
**Moderate** (autonomic instability, fever <41.1°C): Aggressively correct cardiorespiratory & thermal abnormalities, continue benzodiazepines, & add a 5HT2A antagonist such as cyproheptadine.
**Severe** (temp >41.1°C): Immediate sedation, nondepolarizing paralysis, orotracheal intubation, ventilation, & aggressive cooling; premature release of paralysis can allow hyperthermia to recur.
**Agitation Mgmt**: Use benzodiazepines. Avoid physical restraints b/c isometric muscle activity worsens lactic acidosis & hyperthermia.
Autonomic instability: Hypotension: norepinephrine, phenylephrine, or epinephrine. Hypertension/tachycardia: use short-acting agents such as esmolol or nitroprusside.
Hyperthermia: This is from muscle activity, not hypothalamic setpoint change; antipyretics have no role.
Avoid: succinylcholine, propranolol, bromocriptine, dantrolene, & prolonged physical restraints.
Disposition trigger: Moderate severe illness, escalating autonomic instability, hyperthermia, for intubation, or rhabdomyolysis requires ICUlevel care.
Ongoing care: Trend CK, renal function, temperature, & urine output;don't restart serotonergic agents until fully recovered.
**Cyproheptadine**: For moderate-severe disease: 12 mg PO/NG initially, then 2 mg q2h until improvement, then 8 mg q6h maintenance; total 12-32 mg in 24h.
--Parenteral 5HT2A antagonists: If enteral cyproheptadine cannot be used, chlorpromazine IM or olanzapine SL are possible alternatives, though evidence is limited.
Most cases resolve within 24–72 hours after stopping offending agent
Monitor CK q6–12h: trend for Rhabdo
Aggressive IV fluids to maintain UOP >1 mL/kg/h if CK elevated
Serial neuro checks: document clonus resolution
Do NOT restart serotonergic agents until fully resolved. Pharmacy consult for alternatives.
Watch for DIC if severe: serial coags, fibrinogen, Ddimer
**Stat:** Fingerstick glucose, BMP, CBC, CK (Rhabdo), lactate, VBG
**Routine:** LFTs, Mg, PO4, UA (myoglobinuria), PT/PTT/INR (DIC screen)

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP (glucose, Na+), CBC, ABG (if hypoxic), toxicology screen, UA, blood cultures (if febrile)
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2, telemetry, safe environment (remove harmful objects), security/sitter
Call for help early if violence risk; clear the room of unnecessary staff & dangerous objects
Use verbal deescalation, simple commands, lowstimulation environment, & 1:1 observation if needed
If the pt isescalating or cannot be redirected, prepare for chemical sedation & higher level monitoring
Immediate goal: Protect the pt & staff while identifying a medical, neurologic, toxic, or withdrawal cause.
Safety risk: If the pt is attempting harm, pulling lines, eloping, or cannot be verbally redirected, escalate quickly to security, sitter, & chemical sedation.
Deescalation first: Use calm verbal redirection, one speaker, reduced stimulation, familiar staff/family if helpful, & avoid escalating confrontation.
Restraints: Use only if required for immediate safety & pair with rapid reassessment plus treatment of the underlying cause.
Medical causes first: Treat hypoxia, ↓ glucose, infection, pain, urinary retention, constipation, withdrawal, stroke, or seizure before labeling this primary psychiatric agitation.

Medication strategy: PO is preferred when feasible. For parenteral rapid tranquilization, droperidol or olanzapine are preferred first line options; avoid haloperidol in Parkinsonism or Lewy body disease.
Etiologyspecific sedation: Alcohol/sedative withdrawal or stimulant intoxication: benzodiazepines may preferred. Delirium & known psychiatric illness: antipsychotics are preferred.
Combination thetherapy: Antipsychotic + benzodiazepine is not routine b/c adverse effects increase without clear general benefit, though select severe cases may use a monitored combination strategy.
Ketamine: Reserve IM ketamine 2-5 mg/kg as secondline for extreme violence, failed first line sedation, or for immediate control.
Monitoring: After sedation, do close observation with frequent vitals, sedation level checks, pulse ox without routine supplemental O2 masking decline, & EtCO2 when available.

items: Preceding illness 1-4 wks ago: URI, GI illness ( Campylobacter jejuni: most common trigger), CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, Zika, COVID, influenza
Recent vaccination (rare association)
Symptom onset & progression: ascending weakness starting in legs, progressing over days to weeks. Peak sx at 2-4 wks
Sensory sx: paressias, numbness (often precede weakness), pain (esp back/thighs)
Cranial nerve involvement: facial weakness (bilateral), dysphagia, dysarthria, ophthalmoplegia
Autonomic sx: palpitations, urinary retention, constipation, diaphoresis, orthostasis
Prior episodes (recurrent GBS rare: if ≥3 relapses, consider CIDP)
Baseline ambulation status & rate of decline
Meds: BB (worsen ↓ HR in dysautonomia), neuromuscular blockers to avoid

sections.title: Presentation/Exam
items: **Classic presentation**: Symmetric ascending flaccid weakness + areflexia beginning 2–4 weeks after GI or URI infection; autonomic instability and respiratory failure are life-threatening — trend NIF and FVC serially
Symmetric ascending weakness: legs > arms. Grade strength (MRC scale 0-5) in all limbs
Areflexia or hyporeflexia: required finding. Check biceps, triceps, patellar, Achilles
Respiratory assessment: count to 20 in single breath (if can't reach 10-12, concerning), singlebreath count, cough strength, accessory muscle use
Neck flexor weakness: correlates with diaphragmatic involvement & intubation risk
Cranial nerves: facial weakness (CN VII,bilateral), bulbar function (swallow, gag, tongue), extraocular movements (MillerFisher)
Sensory exam: glovestocking paressias, vibration & proprioception (often preserved early)
Autonomic signs: resting tachycardia, BP lability, pupillary dysfunction, ileus, urinary retention
check trajectory: is pt getting better or worse? Hourly trend matters more than single exam

pairs.value: Acute immunemed. polyneuropathy: postinfectious autoimmune attack on peripheral nerves. MCC of acute flaccid paralysis
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: most common subtype (85-90%). Demyelination of motor & sensory nerves
Acute motor axonal neuropathy: motoronly,postCampylobacter. Axonal subtype. Higher intubation risk & slower recovery
Acute motor & sensory axonal neuropathy: combined motor + sensory axonal involvement. More severe
Variant: ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia. Descending pattern. AntiGQ1b antibodies. Generally milder course
CSF: ↑ protein (>45 mg/dL) with nl. WBC (<10 cells/μL). Classic finding but may nl. in first week. >50 WBC suggests alternative dx
Improvementthendeterioration within 8 wks (up to 10% of pts). Retreat with original modality. ≥3 relapses: consider CIDP

sections.title: Autonomic Instability
items: Occurs in~50% of GBS pts: can life-threatening. Telemetry mandatory
Labile BP:severe HTN to ↓ BP. Avoid aggressive tx: episodestransient
Hypertensive episodes: txt stimuli (pain, full bladder, agitation). Shortacting IV vasodilators (nicardipine, clevidipine). Avoid BB (↑ ↓ HR risk)
↓ HR: can progress to asystole. Avoid vagal stimuli (suctioning). D/C negative chronotropes. IV atropine at bedside. External pacing if refractory
Tachycardia:sinus: may not need tx. Check for pain, fever, PE, hypovolemia first
Urinary retention: Foley catheter, bladder scans
Gastroparesis/ileus: promotility agents, consider postpyloric feeding. Aggressive bowel regimen
Acute colonic pseudoObst.: neostigmine (pretreat with glycopyrrolate 0.4mg: neostigmine 2mg IV over 5 min)
Complications: PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) & Takotsubo cardiomyopathy from dysautonomic hypertensive episodes
PEARL: disease plateaus, then improves.don't retreat if improving

pairs.value: Campylobacter jejuni (most common), CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, influenza, COVID19, Zika, hepatitis E, recent surgery, vaccination (rare)
Transverse myelitis, spinal cord compression, myasnia gravis, botulism, poliomyelitis, tick paralysis, critical illness polyneuropathy, hypokalemic periodic paralysis
Sensory level, bladder dysfunction early, UMN signs (hyperreflexia). GBS = LMN (areflexia)
Fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia. Reflexes preserved. No sensory involvement
Descending paralysis (opposite of GBS), dilated pupils, early bulbar involvement, GI prodrome
Back pain, sensory level, UMN signs, bowel/bladder dysfunction. MRI spine diagnostic
Ascending paralysis similar to GBS: search for embedded tick (scalp, hairline). Resolves with tick removal
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: if sx progress >8 wks or ≥3 relapses, reclassify from GBS to CIDP

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** CSF (elevated protein, normal cells), CBC, BMP, anti-ganglioside Ab (GQ1b, GM1), NCS referral
-**Basic labs:** BMP (lytes, Cr), CBC, LFTs, CK, ESR/CRP, TSH. Stool culture for Campylobacter. HIV, Lyme if risk factors
-**ABG/VBG:** If respiratory distress or declining FVC: rising PaCO2 is late finding, do NOT rely on gas alone
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2 (NIF q4-6h — intubate if NIF < -25 cmH2O), Foley (autonomic dysfunction), telemetry, neurology consult
Measure FVC & NIF at bedside: repeat q4-6h (q2h if declining). Trend > single value
**Step 1**: prevent respiratory failure: Trend FVC & NIF closely, repeat airway exams, involve RT early, & move to ICU or intubation based on trajectory not waiting for a late gas change.

**Step 2**: start diseasedirected thetherapy: Start IVIG or PLEX early once GBS is strongly suspected;don't wait for LP/EMG. Choose one modality based on access, hemodynamics, renal function, & local resources; combined IVIG + PLEX is not routinely beneficial.

**Step 3**: supportive & autonomic care: Use telemetry & frequent BP monitoring, give DVT prophylaxis, manage neuropathic pain, monitor swallowing/nutrition, prevent pressure injuries, & avoid succinylcholine or delays in thetherapy.

**FVC (forced vital capacity):** Most important test. Measure q4-6h (q2h if declining). Trend > single value. <20 mL/kg = ICU. <15 mL/kg = consider intubation. <10 mL/kg = strong indication for intubation
**NIF (negative insp force):** < −30 cmH2O = concerning. < −20 cmH2O = intubation likely. Trend alongside FVC
**LP:** Albuminocytologic dissociation: ↑ protein (>45), WBC <10. May be nl. in first week (80-90% sens after wk 1). >50 WBC: consider HIV, Lyme, sarcoid, lymphoma
**EMG/NCS:** Confirms dx & subtype (demyelinating vs axonal). May be nl. <1-2 wks after onset. nl. study >1-2 wks postonset argues against GBS
**MRI spine:** Selective enhancement of anterior spinal nerve roots is suggestive. Also r/o cord compression
**Antiganglioside antibodies:** AntiGQ1b (MillerFisher), antiGM1 (AMAN). Not required for dx but can help with subtyping
**Telemetry:** cardiac monitoring: dysautonomia causes ↓ HR, tachycardia, asystole
**EtCO2:** If available: rising trend with declining FVC suggests impending resp failure

sections.title: Respiratory Monitoring & Intubation
items: FVC & NIF are key bedside tests: measure on admission,thenq4-6h (q2h if declining). ABG/VBG is late indicator
Rough thresholds (integrate with clinical picture: se are NOT absolute cutoffs):
FVC <20 mL/kg: ICU admission
FVC <15 mL/kg: prepare for intubation
FVC <10 mL/kg: strong indication for intubation
NIF weaker than −30 cmH2O: concerning. Weaker than −20 cmH2O: intubation likely
>30% decline in FVC or NIF from baseline: ICU transfer
Clinical signs matter most: ↑ WOB, inability to cough, secretion management difficulty, ↓ singlebreath count, neck flexor weakness, bulbar dysfunction
Do NOT rely on ABG alone: rising PaCO2 is LATE finding. By n, pt may crash during intubation
Preintubation: avoid succinylcholine (↑K). Use rocuronium. Have pushdose epinephrine ready for vagal episodes
Consider early elective intubation not emergent: GBS pts decompensate rapidly
Consider early tracheostomy (~1 wk) in pts with severe weakness, AMAN subtype, or rapid progression: improves comfort, mobilization, oral hygiene

drugs.name: IVIG
drugs.contraindications: IgA deficiency (anaphylaxis risk: check IgA level), severe renal insufficiency
drugs.notes: Firstline: start on clinical dx,don't wait for LP/EMG. Risks: thromboembolism, aseptic meningitis, renal injury, hemolysis. Repeat course within 1-2 wks not beneficial

drugs.name: Plasmapheresis (PLEX)
drugs.dose: 5 exchanges over 1-2 wks (typically 200-250 mL/kg total plasma volume)
drugs.contraindications: Hemodynamic instability (relative), sepsis, active bleeding, poor vascular access
drugs.notes: best if started within 7 days s/s. Equal efficacy to IVIG. More hemodynamic instability but ↓ relapse rate. Preferred in some centers. Requires central line. Combined IVIG + PLEX NOT superior

drugs.name: Gabapentin
drugs.dose: 300mg PO daily, titrate up to 1200mg TID as tolerated
drugs.contraindications: Severe renal insufficiency (adjust dose)
drugs.notes: Firstline for neuropathic pain (very common in GBS). Can also use pregabalin. Sedation may limit dose

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.contraindications: Tachycardia, acute angleclosure glaucoma
drugs.notes: For symptomatic ↓ HR from dysautonomia. Have at bedside for all GBS pts with autonomic instability. Consider external pacing if refractory

drugs.name: Nicardipine or Clevidipine
drugs.dose: Nicardipine 5-15 mg/h IV; Clevidipine 1-2 mg/h IV titrate
drugs.contraindications: Severe aortic stenosis (clevidipine)
drugs.notes: Shortacting IV CCB for hypertensive episodes from dysautonomia. Avoid BB (↑ ↓ HR risk). Transition to PO CCB if sustained

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.dose: 40mg SC daily (or 30mg SC BID if high risk)
drugs.contraindications: Active bleeding, HIT, CrCl <30 (use UFH)
drugs.notes: DVT prophylaxis: immobile pts athigh VTE risk. Start early. Add SCDs

drugs.name: Neostigmine
drugs.dose: 2mg IV over 5 min (pretreat with glycopyrrolate 0.4mg IV)
drugs.contraindications: Mechanical bowel Obst., peritonitis
drugs.notes: For acute colonic pseudoObst. (Ogilvie syndrome) from autonomic dysfunction. Use cautiously: worsens ↓ HR

items: Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC (up to 60 L/min, FiO2 up to 100%) → NIPPV → intubation
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; ↓BP, then tension PTX, PE, or cardiogenic shock
Put on cardiac monitor
Check fingerstick glucose.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: Known MG? How long? AChR vs MuSK? Prior thymoma or thymectomy?
Current regimen: pyridostigmine dose, steroids, immunosuppressants, missed doses, abrupt taper, or recent med change
Common triggers: infection, aspiration, surgery/anesthesia, pregnancy/postpartum, heat, stress, thyroid disease, Ca/Phos/Mg issues

Review every med for MGworsening agents: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, clindamycin, vancomycin, BB, procainamide, quinidine, lithium, phenytoin, antipsychotics, magnesium, iodinated contrast
Recent steroid start or dose increase can temporarily make weakness worse
Prior crisis, prior intubation, prior PLEX vs IVIG, & what response was seen
Bulbar sx: dysphagia, dysarthria, nasal voice, aspiration, weak cough, trouble clearing secretions
Crisis can be the first presentation of MG: keep it on the list in unexplained hypercarbic weakness

pairs.value: ~50% present with purely ocular MG. ~60% have asymmetric ptosis, diplopia, or both as the first sign. Ptosis occurs in ~90% over the disease course. Ice-pack test, prolonged-upgaze test, and single breath count <20 are useful bedside aids.
17–50% generalize within 6–12 months; 61–85% within 2 years; ~85% ultimately develop generalized MG. Only ~16% generalize after 2 years.
Dysarthria, dysphonia/hoarseness, chewing difficulty, dysphagia, nasal voice, reduced facial expression. Neck flexors often involved with bulbar/chest disease.
Proximal > distal (shoulders, upper arms, hips, thighs). Reflexes, sensation, pupils, and autonomic exam should be normal — if abnormal, reconsider the diagnosis.

Crisis occurs in ~13–23%, mostly early in disease. Warning signs: tachypnea, shallow breathing, orthopnea, weak cough, pausing mid-sentence, paradoxical abdominal motion. Serial FVC and NIF are essential — SpO₂ can stay normal until late; rising CO₂ is the earlier alarm.
General fatigue 67%, eye-muscle weakness 59%, drooping eyelids 55%, arm weakness 53% (multinational cohort, MG-ADL). Eyelid fatigability and breathing difficulty are the most functionally limiting.

sections.title: Atypical Presentations (~7% of MG)
items: **Isolated dropped head** (neck extensor weakness) — often MuSK+ or late-onset AChR+; rarely accompanies hiccups
**Bilateral facial weakness** — can be the sole presentation
**Distal limb weakness** — foot drop, hand drop; forearm, finger, or lower-leg extensor weakness
**Isolated limb-girdle weakness** without oculobulbar signs (~4% of MG) — frequently misdiagnosed as polymyositis (CK is normal) or muscular dystrophy
**Ocular without classic ptosis** — pseudo-INO, pseudo-sixth nerve palsy, vertical deviation, esotropia, vergence anomalies
**Focal bulbar/respiratory onset** — tongue weakness/atrophy, dysphonia, stridor from vocal cord paralysis; more common in MuSK+; isolated respiratory presentations delay diagnosis
**Non-motor** — autonomic, cognitive, psychiatric, sensory, GI, sleep disturbances; central fatigue (distinct from fatigability) reported in 44–82%
Atypical presentations are associated with higher MuSK-Ab prevalence and more frequent rituximab use

pairs.value: Weakness worsening with sustained/repetitive activity and improving with rest is the hallmark of MG.
Asymmetry helps distinguish MG from congenital myasthenic syndromes. Bilateral involvement without sensory loss or muscle wasting is the typical pattern in focal presentations.
Separates MG from LEMS (hyporeflexia, dysautonomia, leg-predominant weakness, ocular sparing, facilitation >100% on high-frequency RNS).
Small, short-duration MUAPs with normal CK should prompt RNS and SFEMG rather than a myopathy workup.

AChR Ab: ~80–85% of generalized, ~50% of ocular MG. MuSK Ab: 5–8%. LRP4: ~2%. ~5–7% seronegative. RNS (decremental response); SFEMG (increased jitter): confirms ~90% of seronegative cases. Ice-pack test for ptosis. CT/MRI chest in all patients to screen for thymoma.

Infection is the leading trigger. Others: med changes, nonadherence, surgery/anesthesia, steroids, stress, heat, thyroid disease, pregnancy/postpartum, and electrolyte shifts. Sometimes no trigger is found.
Myasthenic crisis usually has normal pupils and lacks prominent muscarinic findings. Cholinergic crisis points more toward miosis, sweating, bradycardia, fasciculations, and heavy secretions.
MG often starts ocular/bulbar and gets worse with repetition; reflexes stay normal. LEMS usually starts in the legs, may briefly improve after use, has low reflexes, and often includes autonomic sx.
Think about botulism, GBS, ALS, organophosphate toxicity, tick paralysis, brainstem stroke, spinal cord disease, and periodic paralysis.
Do not miss ACS, arrhythmia, sepsis, hypoglycemia, anemia, dehydration, thyroid disease, electrolyte problems, or another cause of respiratory failure.

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** ABG/VBG, CBC, BMP, AChR Ab, anti-MuSK Ab
-**Orders:** IV access, continuous SpO2 (NIF and FVC q4-6h), telemetry, bedside spirometry, neurology consult, IVIG or plasma exchange setup
Watch the breathing trend, not a single number: serial FVC/NIF, capnography, secretion burden, bulbar weakness, cough, and WOB. Do not rely on SpO2 alone.
Use NIV only if the pt is protecting the airway and can clear secretions. If bulbar function is poor or the numbers are falling, choose elective intubation before things crash.
If intubating, try to avoid paralytics if feasible. If needed, use lowdose rocuronium 0.5-0.6 mg/kg; if succinylcholine is chosen, higher doses may be needed. Have sugammadex ready.
Find and treat the trigger at once: infection/aspiration, med exposure, steroid change, surgery/anesthesia, thyroid disease, electrolyte issues, or missed MG meds.

Stop drugs that worsen MG, avoid magnesium, and if the pt is intubated, hold pyridostigmine until extubation is closer. If not intubated, keep home pyridostigmine going unless cholinergic crisis is a real concern.
Start immune therapy early with neurology. PLEX is often chosen first in crisis because it works faster; IVIG is a reasonable alternative when PLEX is not practical.
Be cautious with steroids: keep the home dose if already taking them, but new steroid escalation can transiently worsen weakness, so timing should be deliberate.
**Serial resp tests:** FVC & NIF q2h or more often, plus capnography, secretion burden, & single breath count.
**ABG/VBG:** Hypercapnia (pCO2 >45) is concerning; do not rely on SpO2 alone.
**Basic labs:** CBC, BMP/CMP, Mg, Phos, CRP if infection suspected.
**Trigger workup:** CXR, cultures if infection is suspected, thyroid studies, med review, aspiration evaluation.
**MG workup:** AChR Ab, MuSK Ab, CT chest for thymoma. Do not delay crisis treatment while waiting.
**Monitoring:** Telemetry & pulse ox; airway/aspiration precautions.

drugs.name: IVIG
drugs.contraindications: Renal failure, IgA deficiency (anaphylaxis risk)
drugs.notes: Diseasemodifying: effect lasts 30-45 days; onset slower than PLEX (days to weeks). Easier to give (peripheral IV ok)

drugs.name: Plasmapheresis (PLEX)
drugs.contraindications: Hemodynamic instability, limited access, major coagulopathy
drugs.notes: Fastest onset: improvement often by the 2nd-3rd session. Generally preferred in crisis if feasible.

drugs.name: Pyridostigmine
drugs.dose: 30-60 mg PO q4-6h (max 90 mg q4h); IV: 2-3 mg (1/30th PO dose)
drugs.contraindications: Cholinergic crisis, mechanical ileus
drugs.notes: Symptomatic only. Stop if intubated to reduce secretions; restart near extubation. If not intubated, abrupt cessation can worsen weakness.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone / Prednisone
drugs.contraindications: Active uncontrolled infection (relative)
drugs.notes: If already taking steroids, continue. New initiation can transiently worsen weakness, especially in the first 5-10 days.

pairs.value: Autoimmune NMJ disorder, most often from AChR antibodies. Weakness is fatigable: worse with repeated use, better after rest.
Severe MG flare causing respiratory failure or airway risk, often requiring intubation. Many crises happen early in the disease course.
Too much acetylcholinesterase inhibitor causing weakness plus muscarinic excess. Rare now, but still worth distinguishing from true crisis.
Intubation, with or without full ventilator support, qualifies as MGFA Class V.
Normal ≥60 mL/kg. <20 mL/kg or rapid decline = impending respiratory failure
Normal about 80 to 100 cmH₂O. Weaker than 30 cmH₂O = significant respiratory weakness

sections.title: Important Points
items: Reflexes, sensation, pupils, and autonomic findings should stay normal in MG: abnormalities push you toward another diagnosis.
SpO2 can stay normal until late: worsening ventilation often shows up first as rising CO2, weak cough, and poor secretion clearance.
PLEX and IVIG both work; PLEX is often favored in crisis because the response is quicker.
Avoid magnesium: it can noticeably worsen NMJ transmission and tip a borderline pt into respiratory failure.
Thymic disease is common in MG, but thymectomy is a longgame issue, not the priority in the acute crisis window.

sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: !!Check fingerstick glucose
Airway: patent? suction if secretions/vomit; jaw thrust if obstructed
-If rapidly declining, can’t protect airway, or GCS falling: !!call ICU + anesthesia now!!, prepare for intubation
Breathing: RR, SpO2 (good pleth?), WOB — !!normal SpO2 does NOT exclude hypercarbia!!
-Get VBG/ABG in any obtunded patient or suspected CO2 retention
Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; severely hypertensive or shock? Arrhythmia on monitor?
Put on cardiac monitor now
Temperature: fever → infection/NMS/serotonin syndrome; hypothermia → myxedema/toxin/exposure
Pupils: anisocoria, pinpoint (opioid), mydriasis (anticholinergic/sympathomimetic)
Rapid focal neuro exam: gaze deviation, facial asymmetry, unilateral weakness, aphasia → !!stroke protocol!!
Seizure clues: rhythmic twitching, eyelid flutter, gaze deviation, unexplained staring
!!MAR review now!!: opioids, sedatives, anticholinergics, cefepime, baclofen, gabapentinoids
Bedside sequence: !!Glucose → O2/ventilation → pupils → focal neuro → vitals/temp → MAR → bladder scan!!

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: !!What changed in the last 24–72 hours?!! — the cause is usually here
Baseline mentation from family — 'new vs. baseline' is everything
**Acuity**: sudden onset → structural/vascular; hours → metabolic/toxic/infection; days → subacute
!!Review the MAR yourself!!: every medication given in prior 48–72h; cross-reference renal/hepatic function
**Chronic med changes**: dose changes, new starts, abrupt stops (benzos, baclofen, clonidine, opioids, dopaminergics)
**Urinary retention**: common, reversible delirium trigger — bladder scan early
**Constipation**: common in elderly + dementia
**Pain, sleep deprivation**: common hospital precipitants
**Nutritional status**: malnutrition, NPO, bariatric surgery, alcohol → Wernicke risk
Alcohol, benzo, baclofen, opioid, clonidine use — withdrawal can begin within hours of admission

pairs.value: Not a diagnosis — usually multifactorial. Identify immediately reversible threats (glucose, opioids, seizure, herniation) while building the full picture.
Ischemic stroke, ICH, SDH, SAH, seizure/NCSE, postictal, meningitis, encephalitis, PRES, CVST, hydrocephalus. !!Focal deficit → stroke alert immediately!!
Hypoxemia, hypercapnia (!!CO2 narcosis with normal SpO2!!), shock, hypertensive emergency, low cardiac output
Hypo/hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, hypoglycemia, hyperglycemia, Mg, phosphate, acid-base disorders, uremia, hepatic failure, thyroid/adrenal disease
Sepsis, pneumonia, abdominal infection, CNS infection, autoimmune encephalitis. !!Bacteriuria ≠ UTI!! — delirium + bacteriuria without urinary sx → search for another cause first
Opioids, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, cefepime, baclofen, gabapentinoids, lithium, valproate, alcohol, CO. !!Most common reversible cause in hospitalized adults!! — review the MAR personally
Alcohol (onset 6–24h), benzos, baclofen, clonidine, opioids, dopaminergic drugs. !!Ask specifically about home use on admission!!
Pain, urinary retention, constipation, sleep deprivation, immobility, restraints, dehydration, sensory deprivation — multiple simultaneous insults are the rule in older patients with delirium
Assess: arousal, !!attention!! (months backward, digit span — centerpiece of delirium), commands, language, fluctuation, hallucinations. Motor phenotype: hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed.
The quiet, staring, not-eating patient may have worse delirium than the one climbing out of bed. Inattention and fluctuation are more useful than orientation questions.

Pupils, gaze deviation, facial asymmetry, pronator drift, weakness, aphasia, dysarthria, neglect, cerebellar signs, rigidity/clonus, !!asterixis!! (uremia, hypercapnia, toxic-metabolic — not just hepatic), myoclonus
!!Bladder scan!! — retention is common and treatable. Also: medication patches, skin, lines/drains, neck for meningismus, oxygen delivery device

Rhythmic finger or facial twitching, nystagmus, repetitive chewing, gaze deviation, pupillary fluctuations, waxing/waning responsiveness. !!Do not call someone ‘postictal for 18h’ without reconsidering ongoing NCSE!!

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-!!Fingerstick glucose immediately!! — every patient, every time
--Stat labs: CBC, BMP/CMP, Mg, phosphate, LFTs, VBG, ECG
-Add selectively (not reflexively): blood cultures/lactate, TSH, cortisol, ammonia (specific contexts), tox screen, CK, serum osmolality
-!!VBG/ABG!! if any concern for hypoventilation or hypercapnia — normal SpO2 does not exclude CO2 narcosis
-!!Bladder scan!! — urinary retention is common and treatable
-!!Review the MAR!!: prior 48–72h, cross-reference with current renal and hepatic function
**If hypoglycemia**: D50 25 g IV push or D10 100–250 mL; recheck in 15 min. No IV access: glucagon 1 mg IM
**If opioid toxicity (hypoventilating)**: naloxone 0.04 mg IV in opioid-dependent patients (titrate); 0.4 mg IV/IM/IN otherwise. Repeat q2–3 min PRN. Goal: adequate ventilation, not full arousal
**If active seizure**: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg); may repeat once. Move to institutional SE pathway
**If Wernicke suspected (alcohol, malnutrition, bariatric, hyperemesis)**: !!thiamine 500 mg IV q8h x 3 days!!. Do not wait for the classic triad
**If meningitis/encephalitis suspected**: cultures/LP when feasible but !!do NOT delay antibiotics!!. Add acyclovir if HSV is reasonably suspected
**Imaging**
**CT head**: focal neurologic deficit, abrupt severe AMS, trauma/anticoagulation, new seizure, severe headache, malignancy, immunosuppression, persistently unexplained encephalopathy
-!!Normal CT does NOT rule out neurologic disease!! — misses small/posterior stroke, encephalitis, PRES, CVST, hypoxic injury. Consider MRI if substantial encephalopathy persists after unrevealing CT

EEG when: unexplained persistent AMS, not improving after presumed seizure, recurrent fluctuations, twitching/myoclonus/eyelid flutter, cefepime exposure, prior epilepsy. !!NCSE in 8–30% of selected unexplained AMS cases!!

**LP when**: fever + encephalopathy, meningismus, new seizures, immunocompromised, suspected HSV, subacute behavioral change with neuro findings. Do not require meningismus to consider CNS infection in elderly/immunosuppressed

pairs.value: Review every medication given in the prior 48–72h, including PRNs. Cross-reference with current renal and hepatic function.
Opioids → sedation, hypoventilation, myoclonus. Benzos → delirium, respiratory depression. Both accumulate with renal/hepatic impairment.
Diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, oxybutynin, tolterodine, TCAs, muscle relaxants — classic anticholinergic delirium. Particularly problematic in older adults.
AMS 93%, myoclonus 37%, NCSE ~28%. Almost always with renal dysfunction; onset ~4 days. Stop or dose-reduce, obtain EEG, consider dialysis in severe cases.
Even low doses cause severe encephalopathy when renal clearance falls. GFR <30 → unpredictably prolonged half-life. Abrupt withdrawal also dangerous (seizures).
Renally eliminated. AKI + gabapentin + confusion/myoclonus = drug accumulation until proven otherwise.
Confusion ± vomiting ± ataxia ± worsening seizures on valproate → check ammonia. Occurs without hepatic failure. Hold/reduce valproate; consider levocarnitine in severe toxicity.
Zolpidem, steroids (mania/psychosis), fluoroquinolones (neuropsychiatric), lithium (toxicity even at therapeutic levels), dopaminergic drugs (hallucinations; withdrawal also dangerous)

pairs.key: Wernicke — Treat Before You Prove It
pairs.value: Do not require the classic triad — it is insensitive. Risk: alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, cancer, prolonged poor intake, dialysis. !!Thiamine 500 mg IV TID x 3 days!!, then taper. Replace magnesium — thiamine-dependent enzymes require it.

pairs.key: Hepatic Encephalopathy — Don’t Treat the Ammonia Number
pairs.value: HE is a clinical diagnosis. !!Elevated ammonia does NOT prove HE!!, does NOT grade severity reliably, and serial levels generally do NOT guide treatment (AASLD). Treat the precipitant: GI bleed, infection, constipation, dehydration, AKI, excessive diuresis, sedatives/opioids. Don’t label every confused cirrhotic as ‘HE’ — they can have stroke, meningitis, hypercapnia, drug toxicity, or SDH.

!!SpO2 can be 96% with PaCO2 80 mmHg!!. Suspect in COPD, obesity hypoventilation, OSA, neuromuscular weakness, opioids/sedatives, excess O2 in CO2 retainer. Get VBG. NIV if airway protected; ICU if worsening or NIV failing.

NCSE in 8–30% of selected unexplained AMS. !!Do not call someone postictal for 18h without reconsidering ongoing NCSE!!. Clues: rhythmic twitching, nystagmus, chewing, gaze deviation, waxing/waning consciousness. Lower EEG threshold as the explanation weakens.

Mutism, staring, immobility, posturing, waxy flexibility, refusal to eat, unexplained rigidity. !!Avoid escalating antipsychotics — can worsen and precipitate NMS!!. Lorazepam 1–2 mg IV challenge supports diagnosis. Involve psychiatry/neurology.
Pain, hypoxia/hypercapnia, urinary retention, constipation, withdrawal, sensory impairment, sleep deprivation, unnecessary restraints/lines.

pairs.key: Antipsychotics — Not Proven to Shorten Delirium
pairs.value: SCCM PADIS 2025: evidence insufficient to recommend antipsychotics over usual care for delirium. Reserve for: pulling critical devices, attacking staff, or severe psychotic distress. !!Reassess before stacking doses!!. Check QTc.

SCCM 2025 favors dexmedetomidine over propofol for light sedation when reducing delirium is a priority. Infusion: 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/hr. Watch for bradycardia/hypotension. Onset too slow for acute violent behavior.

sections.title: When to Escalate to ICU
items: Inability to protect airway
Rapidly declining consciousness or GCS
Hypercapnic or hypoxic respiratory failure
Status epilepticus or NCSE requiring continuous treatment
New focal neurologic deficit or stroke syndrome
Suspected increased ICP or herniation
Severe agitation requiring continuous IV sedation
Severe alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal
Meningitis/encephalitis with deterioration
Shock of any etiology
Severe hyponatremia (<120) requiring close correction
NMS/serotonin syndrome/malignant catatonia
Severe toxic ingestion or acute hyperammonemia with seizure

drugs.name: Dextrose (D50)
drugs.dose: 25 g IV push; D10 100–250 mL as gentler alternative
drugs.contraindications: Extravasation causes tissue necrosis — confirm good IV before pushing D50
drugs.notes: Hypoglycemia or high clinical suspicion. D10 is safer peripherally and avoids rebound spikes. Recheck in 15 min.

drugs.name: Thiamine
drugs.dose: Wernicke suspected: 500 mg IV TID x 3 days, then 200–500 mg IV daily. Empiric/prophylactic: 100 mg IV
drugs.contraindications: Hypersensitivity (rare anaphylaxis with IV/IM)
drugs.notes: Give in all patients with alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, bariatric surgery, hyperemesis, or prolonged poor intake. Do not wait for the classic triad. Also replace magnesium — thiamine-dependent enzymes require it.

drugs.name: Haloperidol
drugs.dose: Frail/elderly: 0.5–1 mg PO/IM; typical adult: 1–2 mg. Reassess before stacking
drugs.contraindications: Parkinsonism/Lewy body dementia (can precipitate severe EPS), QTc >500 ms
drugs.notes: First-line IV/IM for agitation. Highest QTc risk. Check QTc and electrolytes. Reassess before redosing.

drugs.name: Olanzapine
drugs.contraindications: QTc prolongation, NMS history, caution in elderly and DM
drugs.notes: Useful when EPS is a concern. !!Do NOT combine IM olanzapine with IV/IM benzodiazepines!! — risk of cardiorespiratory depression.

drugs.name: Quetiapine
drugs.contraindications: QTc prolongation, NMS history, caution in elderly
drugs.notes: Oral only. Favored when parkinsonism/EPS is a concern. Lowest QTc risk among antipsychotics.

drugs.name: Aripiprazole
drugs.contraindications: NMS history; caution in seizure disorders
drugs.notes: Lowest QTc risk. Use if QTc >500 or multiple QTc-prolonging agents present.

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
drugs.dose: 0.2–0.7 mcg/kg/hr IV infusion; avoid loading dose in unstable patients
drugs.contraindications: Severe bradycardia, high-degree AV block without pacing, severe hypotension
drugs.notes: ICU use: preferred when agitation prevents ventilator weaning/extubation (SCCM 2025). Watch for bradycardia and hypotension. Not for acute violent behavior — onset too slow.

drugs.name: Naloxone
drugs.dose: Opioid-dependent + hypoventilating: 0.04 mg IV, titrate. Otherwise: 0.4 mg IV/IM/IN. Repeat q2–3 min PRN
drugs.contraindications: Precipitates acute withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients
drugs.notes: Titrate to adequate ventilation, not full arousal. Shorter half-life than most opioids — re-sedation may occur; monitor closely.

drugs.name: Flumazenil
drugs.dose: 0.2 mg IV over 15 sec, may repeat carefully
drugs.contraindications: Chronic benzo use, seizure disorder, mixed overdose
drugs.notes: Rarely indicated; can precipitate refractory seizures. Use only with clear benzo-only exposure in a benzo-naive patient.

drugs.name: Hypertonic saline 3%
drugs.dose: 100 mL IV bolus, may repeat up to 3 times
drugs.contraindications: Hypernatremia, volume overload; avoid rapid correction (central pontine myelinolysis risk)
drugs.notes: Symptomatic hyponatremic encephalopathy with seizure, severe confusion, or coma. Target: raise Na by ~5 mEq/L to relieve symptoms; do not fully correct rapidly.

drugs.name: Lorazepam
drugs.dose: Active seizure/SE: 0.1 mg/kg IV (max 4 mg), may repeat once. CIWA/withdrawal: per protocol
drugs.contraindications: Respiratory depression without airway support; avoid for ordinary delirium
drugs.notes: First-line for active seizure/status epilepticus and alcohol/benzo withdrawal. Also first-line for catatonia. Avoid in ordinary delirium.

drugs.name: Levetiracetam (Keppra)
drugs.contraindications: Dose-adjust for renal failure
drugs.notes: Second-line after benzodiazepine for seizure/status; also used when nonconvulsive status is suspected and further sedation is undesirable.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin
drugs.dose: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + pharmacy-dosed vancomycin
drugs.contraindications: Cephalosporin or vancomycin allergy; renal failure (vancomycin dose-adjust)
drugs.notes: Empiric bacterial meningitis. Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV with or before first dose.

drugs.name: Ampicillin
drugs.contraindications: Penicillin allergy
drugs.notes: Add for Listeria coverage: age >50, pregnancy, immunocompromise.

drugs.name: Acyclovir
drugs.dose: 10 mg/kg IV q8h (dose-adjust for renal function)
drugs.contraindications: Renal dysfunction without dose adjustment
drugs.notes: Add when HSV encephalitis is reasonably suspected (behavioral change, aphasia, temporal seizures, temporal MRI findings). Do not wait for LP result.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.contraindications: Active untreated infection (relative — do not delay in bacterial meningitis)
drugs.notes: Give with or before first antibiotic dose if bacterial meningitis suspected. Reduces neurologic complications.

drugs.name: Lactulose
drugs.dose: 30–45 mL PO/NG q1–2h until 2–3 BMs, then titrate to 2–3 soft BMs/day
drugs.contraindications: Bowel obstruction
drugs.notes: First-line for hepatic encephalopathy. Avoid overtreating to diarrhea — dehydration worsens HE.

drugs.name: Rifaximin
drugs.contraindications: Severe hepatic impairment (relative), intestinal obstruction
drugs.notes: Add-on for recurrent or persistent hepatic encephalopathy. Use in addition to lactulose, not instead.

items: **Classic presentation**: Red flag headaches warrant urgent workup: thunderclap onset (SAH), worst of life, new with fever/neck stiffness (meningitis), progressive over weeks, or associated with focal deficits or papilledema
Vitals: fever, severe HTN, abnormal respirations
Neuro exam: focal deficits, speech, mentation, gait, cranial nerves
Fundoscopy if possible: papilledema or retinal hemorrhage
Meningeal signs: nuchal rigidity, photophobia
Temporal artery / scalp tenderness and jaw claudication features in older adults

pairs.value: Worst headache of life, maximal at onset, vomiting, meningismus, collapse
Unilateral, pulsating, nausea/photophobia, aura possible. Sumatriptan, ketorolac, prochlorperazine, IV fluids.
B/l, band-like, no nausea/photophobia. NSAIDs, acetaminophen.
Unilateral periorbital, autonomic features (lacrimation, rhinorrhea). 100% O2, sumatriptan SQ, verapamil for prevention.
Age >50, temporal tenderness, jaw claudication, ESR >50. Prednisone 40-60mg immediately — do not wait for biopsy.
Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia

sections.title: Management
items: CHECK NOW
-**Labs:** BMP, CBC, coags (if considering LP), ESR/CRP (if GCA suspected)
-**Orders:** CT head w/o contrast (stat if thunderclap/worst HA of life), IV access, continuous SpO2
If thunderclap HA:!!STAT non-contrast head CT!! → if negative → LP for xanthochromia (r/o SAH)
If focal deficits: consider stroke alert (CT, CTA)
If fever + nuchal rigidity: empiric meningitis tx BEFORE LP (vanc + ceftriaxone + dexamethasone)
**Non-contrast CT head:** Immediate for thunderclap headache, neuro deficits, anticoagulation, trauma, ↓ LOC, or other red flags
**LP:** If CT negative but SAH or meningitis still suspected — xanthochromia, RBCs, opening pressure, cell count, protein, glucose, cultures
**CTA head / neck:** If SAH suspected/confirmed, dissection concern, or vascular lesion needs localization
**CBC / BMP / coags:** Check infection, anemia, electrolytes, anticoagulation-related hemorrhage risk
**ESR / CRP:** If giant cell arteritis is suspected
**Pregnancy test / tox / CO:** Based on context: pregnancy-related headache, intoxication, or carbon monoxide exposure

sections.title: The First 60 Seconds
items: Circulation: HR, BP, perfusion; ↓BP, then tension PTX, PE, or cardiogenic shock
Put on cardiac monitor
Airway: airway patent? Look, listen; suction if secretions/blood; jaw thrust if obstructed; call for airway help early
-If Pt looks terrible, can't protect airway: call ICU + anesthesia, then get ready to intubate
Breathing: RR, SpO2(good pleth?), WOB, accessory muscle use, paradoxical breathing, speaking in full sentences?
Start O2 now: NRB 15 L/min if in distress
Rapid O2 escalation if NRB insufficient: HFNC (up to 60 L/min, FiO2 up to 100%) → NIPPV → intubation
Check fingerstick glucose.

sections.title: Chart Check / Hx.
items: !!Witnessed details!!: manner of collapse, duration, rhythmic movements — rhythmic convulsive movements can occur briefly in syncope too
!!Inciting events!!: prolonged standing, upon standing, stressors, pain, poor PO intake, hot weather, injection/cannulation, cough, micturition, defecation

!!Prodrome!!: dizziness, nausea, abdominal discomfort, warmth/flushing, pallor, tunneling vision — vasovagal likelihood ratios: prolonged standing (+LR 9), abdominal discomfort (+LR 8), injection/cannulation (+LR 7)
!!Recovery!!: time to baseline, confusion, nausea/vomiting — prolonged postictal confusion (>30–60 sec) → seizure; rapid complete recovery → favors syncope
!!Red flags (cardiac etiology)!!: no prodrome, exertional syncope, supine syncope, palpitations/chest pain/SOB before LOC, family hx sudden cardiac death, known structural heart disease
!!Associated symptoms!!: lateral tongue bite (seizure > syncope), incontinence (both — does NOT distinguish), head strike, lucid interval (epidural hematoma)
!!Meds!!: antihypertensives, diuretics, BB, alpha blockers, vasodilators (orthostasis); opioids, benzos, TCAs, EtOH (CNS depression/intoxication)
!!Comorbidities!!: CAD, CHF, valvular disease, arrhythmia hx, DM, Parkinson's, prior syncope, PE risk factors (malignancy, asymmetric leg swelling)

sections.title: Exam
items: !!Orthostatic vitals!!: drop ≥20 SBP or ≥10 DBP within 3 minutes of standing from lying. Also note: HR rise ≥30 suggests POTS. Specify how you want nursing to perform this — they often do it incorrectly.
-Method: BP lying → immediately on standing → 3 minutes standing. 3-min standing most clinically relevant (when patients fall getting out of bed).
-HR/SBP ratio <0.5 = neurogenic orthostasis (Ann Neurol 2018). Neurogenic causes: Parkinson's, Lewy body, MSA/Shy-Drager, amyloid, DM, B12 deficiency.
Cardiac: !!murmur!! (AS — loud systolic murmur at RUSB radiating to carotids; if mod-severe AS present, murmur will be audible — no need to echo to find it), S3, S4, irregular rhythm
Neuro: focal deficits, postictal state, GCS; if stroke suspected → focal = TIA/stroke, not syncope
Volume status: skin turgor, mucous membranes, cap refill, JVP, lower extremity edema

pairs.value: Transient, self-limited LOC with complete spontaneous recovery, loss of postural tone, abrupt onset, and due to cerebral hypoperfusion (i.e., transient hypotension). Excludes: hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication, seizure, stroke — these are LOC mimics, not syncope.
PE, arrhythmia (VT, complete heart block, sick sinus, WPW, long QT, Brugada), aortic stenosis, HOCM, ACS, AAA, seizure, stroke/TIA, hemorrhage, hypoglycemia

Most common. Vagal stimulation → bradycardia + vasodilation → ↓ CO + ↓ BP. Must be triggered. Vasovagal, situational (cough, micturition, defecation, swallow), carotid sinus hypersensitivity, pain/needle phobia.

SBP drop ≥20 or DBP ≥10 within 3 min of standing. Causes: volume depletion (↓ PO, GI losses, hemorrhage), meds (diuretics, vasodilators, BB, alpha blockers), autonomic failure (Parkinson's, Lewy body, MSA/Shy-Drager, amyloid, DM, B12 deficiency).

!!Arrhythmia!!: VT, SVT, AV block, sick sinus, long QT, Brugada, pacer malfunction. !!Structural!!: AS, HOCM, PE, ACS, cardiac tamponade, aortic dissection. If not reflex or orthostatic → cardiac until proven otherwise.

pairs.key: EKG clues in young cardiac syncope
pairs.value: WPW (delta wave, short PR), LVH (HOCM), Brugada (coved ST elevation in V1-V2), long QT (>460 ms women, >440 ms men), ARVC (Epsilon wave, T-wave inversion V1-V3), complete heart block, pre-excitation

Seizure (lateral tongue bite, incontinence, prolonged postictal). Stroke/TIA — vertebrobasilar distribution can cause global hypoperfusion; other distributions rarely cause syncope without focal deficits. Avoid carotid dopplers unless focal neurologic findings are present.
Hypoglycemia, hypoxia, intoxication (EtOH, benzo, opioids), hyperventilation, psychiatric, mechanical fall

Red flags present (cardiac features), new non-sinus EKG rhythm, dyspnea, anemia, hypotension, known heart failure, or structural heart disease. Low-risk reflex/orthostatic syncope with clear etiology may be safely discharged with outpatient follow-up.
CBC, BMP, troponin, NT-proBNP, EKG, telemetry. Also: orthostatic vitals, fingerstick glucose.

Romeo Score: if CHF, CAD, abnormal EKG, hsTNT >14, NT-proBNP >125 are ALL absent → major structural finding as cause of syncope only 0.8% likely (J Hosp Med 2018). Only ~3% of inpatient echos find structural lesions; <1% reveal new AS. If mod-severe AS is present, you will hear the murmur — listen before ordering.
If head strike, anticoagulated patient, focal neurologic deficit, or concern for intracranial pathology.

PE identified in 17.3% of patients hospitalized with first-episode syncope in one cohort (NEJM 2016) — but included incidental/chronic PE. True incidence of PE causing syncope is likely lower. Obtain if workup is otherwise unremarkable and clinical suspicion for PE exists.

Holter / ZioPatch: continuous 24–48h recording. Event recorder: patient-activated, only records during symptoms (requires patient cooperation). Loop recorder: long-term; continuously overwrites unless patient presses button after event (keeps data leading up to trigger). Implantable loop recorder for highest-yield long-term monitoring.
Outpatient tilt table test. If orthostatic: consider A1C, SPEP, RPR, B12 to investigate underlying cause of autonomic neuropathy.

sections.title: Management
items: If not appearing hypervolemic and low concern for CHF → give IV fluid bolus
Hold antihypertensives and diuretics until volume status is assessed
**Reflex/vasovagal:** Avoid provocative stimuli; trial counterpressure maneuvers (leg crossing, hand grip, Valsalva) at onset of prodrome
**Orthostatic hypotension — non-pharmacologic:** replete volume; slow positional changes; waist-high compression stockings; abdominal binder; increased dietary salt

**Orthostatic hypotension — pharmacologic:** midodrine 5–10 mg PO TID during waking hours (not within 4h of bedtime — supine hypertension); fludrocortisone 0.1–0.2 mg PO QD; droxidopa for neurogenic orthostasis
-Discontinue or reduce offending medications (diuretics, vasodilators, BB, alpha blockers)
**Cardiac syncope:** address underlying arrhythmia or structural cause — cardiology referral, pacing, ablation, valvular intervention as appropriate
Delegate history and chart review to a teammate while stabilizing

sections.title: Pearls & Pitfalls
items: **Urine incontinence does NOT distinguish syncope from seizure** — it occurs in both. Classic teaching was unreliable.
**Lateral tongue bite suggests seizure; frontal bite suggests syncope** — this too is NOT validated. Do not rely on tongue bite location alone.
**If it's not reflex or orthostatic, assume cardiac** until proven otherwise — cardiac syncope carries the highest mortality risk.

**POTS:** HR rise ≥30 bpm upon standing with orthostatic symptoms (without sufficient BP drop to meet orthostasis criteria). Common in young women. Management: volume repletion, compression, beta blockers, ivabradine.

**Carotid dopplers:** generally not useful in syncope without focal neurologic deficits — carotid disease rarely causes global hypoperfusion (vertebrobasilar distribution is the notable exception for TIA-related LOC).
**Orthostasis technique matters:** specify exactly how you want it done — many bedside checks are performed incorrectly. Standard: BP lying → immediately standing → 3 minutes standing.
**AS echo trap:** if moderate-severe AS is present, it will be audible on exam. Ordering echo to 'look for AS' as a cause of syncope without examining is low-yield and expensive.
**EKG in young patients with syncope:** look specifically for delta wave (WPW), Brugada pattern, long QT, Epsilon wave (ARVC), LVH (HOCM) — these can be subtle.

**Ambulatory monitoring:** be specific about the type ordered — a Holter covers 24–48h; an event recorder only captures patient-triggered events; a loop recorder (external or implantable) is needed for infrequent events.
